review_note: Perfection is local when a derived object has strictly perfect models on a cover, and is independent of the chosen representative. Based on an independent mathematical comparison to the pinned original theorem excerpt in the Stage A record; source proofs/remarks not opened. Preliminary only.
statement:
For a ringed site (C,O), a complex E^bullet is **perfect** when after a covering of every site object it has a quasi-isomorphism from a **strictly perfect** complex (bounded, termwise direct summand of finite free O-modules); a derived object is perfect if represented by such a complex (source Definition perfect at 12734–12746). A perfect object is **not assumed globally bounded** unless the topos is quasi-compact. Its relation to pseudo-coherence and local finite Tor dimension is an equivalence only where stated, not an inherited hypothesis. The first clause assumes a **final object X**, while the second is independent of any such object.

Let $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O})$ be a ringed site.
Let $E$ be an object of $D(\mathcal{O})$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\mathcal{C}$ has a final object $X$ and there exist a
covering $\{U_i \to X\}$, strictly perfect complexes $\mathcal{E}_i^\bullet$
of $\mathcal{O}_{U_i}$-modules, and isomorphisms
 $\alpha_i : \mathcal{E}_i^\bullet \to E|_{U_i}$ in
$D(\mathcal{O}_{U_i})$, then $E$ is perfect.
\item If $E$ is perfect, then any complex representing $E$ is perfect.
\end{enumerate}
hypotheses: (C,O) is a ringed site and E∈D(O).
conclusions: If C has a final object X with a covering {U_i→X} and strictly perfect complexes E_i^bullet and isomorphisms E_i^bullet≅E|_{U_i} in D(O_{U_i}), then E is perfect.
If E is perfect, then **every** complex representing E is perfect.
original_source_statement_tex:
\label{lemma-perfect-independent-representative}
Let $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O})$ be a ringed site.
Let $E$ be an object of $D(\mathcal{O})$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\mathcal{C}$ has a final object $X$ and there exist a
covering $\{U_i \to X\}$, strictly perfect complexes $\mathcal{E}_i^\bullet$
of $\mathcal{O}_{U_i}$-modules, and isomorphisms
 $\alpha_i : \mathcal{E}_i^\bullet \to E|_{U_i}$ in
$D(\mathcal{O}_{U_i})$, then $E$ is perfect.
\item If $E$ is perfect, then any complex representing $E$ is perfect.
\end{enumerate}

review_note: A bounded-Tor-amplitude complex that is sufficiently pseudo-coherent (a−1) is perfect. Based on an independent mathematical comparison to the pinned original theorem excerpt in the Stage A record; source proofs/remarks not opened. Preliminary only.
statement:
For a ringed site (C,O), a complex E^bullet is **perfect** when after a covering of every site object it has a quasi-isomorphism from a **strictly perfect** complex (bounded, termwise direct summand of finite free O-modules); a derived object is perfect if represented by such a complex (source Definition perfect at 12734–12746). A perfect object is **not assumed globally bounded** unless the topos is quasi-compact. Its relation to pseudo-coherence and local finite Tor dimension is an equivalence only where stated, not an inherited hypothesis. The integer shift is **(a−1)-pseudo-coherent** (not a-pseudo-coherent), paired with Tor-amplitude [a,b].

Let $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O})$ be a ringed site.
Let $E$ be an object of $D(\mathcal{O})$.
Let $a \leq b$ be integers. If $E$ has tor amplitude in $[a, b]$
and is $(a - 1)$-pseudo-coherent, then $E$ is perfect.
hypotheses: (C,O) is a ringed site, E∈D(O), a≤b integers.
E has Tor-amplitude [a,b] and E is (a−1)-pseudo-coherent.
original_source_statement_tex:
\label{lemma-perfect-precise}
Let $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O})$ be a ringed site.
Let $E$ be an object of $D(\mathcal{O})$.
Let $a \leq b$ be integers. If $E$ has tor amplitude in $[a, b]$
and is $(a - 1)$-pseudo-coherent, then $E$ is perfect.

review_note: Perfection is equivalent to pseudo-coherence plus local finite Tor dimension. Based on an independent mathematical comparison to the pinned original theorem excerpt in the Stage A record; source proofs/remarks not opened. Preliminary only.
statement:
For a ringed site (C,O), a complex E^bullet is **perfect** when after a covering of every site object it has a quasi-isomorphism from a **strictly perfect** complex (bounded, termwise direct summand of finite free O-modules); a derived object is perfect if represented by such a complex (source Definition perfect at 12734–12746). A perfect object is **not assumed globally bounded** unless the topos is quasi-compact. Its relation to pseudo-coherence and local finite Tor dimension is an equivalence only where stated, not an inherited hypothesis. **Locally** finite Tor dimension requires possibly different intervals after different local covers and does not assert globally finite Tor-amplitude.

Let $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O})$ be a ringed site.
Let $E$ be an object of $D(\mathcal{O})$.
The following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item $E$ is perfect, and
\item $E$ is pseudo-coherent and locally has finite tor dimension.
\end{enumerate}
hypotheses: (C,O) is a ringed site and E∈D(O).
conclusions: E is perfect **iff** E is pseudo-coherent and locally has finite Tor dimension.

review_note: Derived inverse image of a perfect derived O-module remains perfect on any ringed site. Based on an independent mathematical comparison to the pinned original theorem excerpt in the Stage A record; source proofs/remarks not opened. Preliminary only.
statement:
For a ringed site (C,O), a complex E^bullet is **perfect** when after a covering of every site object it has a quasi-isomorphism from a **strictly perfect** complex (bounded, termwise direct summand of finite free O-modules); a derived object is perfect if represented by such a complex (source Definition perfect at 12734–12746). A perfect object is **not assumed globally bounded** unless the topos is quasi-compact. Its relation to pseudo-coherence and local finite Tor dimension is an equivalence only where stated, not an inherited hypothesis. The input E is on the **target** ringed site (D,O_D), and the derived pullback goes to the source site (C,O_C). No flatness of f is required.

Let $(f, f^\sharp) : (\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}) \to
(\mathcal{D}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{D})$
be a morphism of ringed sites.
Let $E$ be an object of $D(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{D})$.
If $E$ is perfect in $D(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{D})$,
then $Lf^*E$ is perfect in $D(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C})$.
hypotheses: f:(C,O_C)→(D,O_D) is a morphism of ringed sites.
original_source_statement_tex:
\label{lemma-perfect-pullback}
Let $(f, f^\sharp) : (\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}) \to
(\mathcal{D}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{D})$
be a morphism of ringed sites.
Let $E$ be an object of $D(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{D})$.
If $E$ is perfect in $D(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{D})$,
then $Lf^*E$ is perfect in $D(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C})$.

review_note: Perfect complexes satisfy distinguished-triangle two-out-of-three. Based on an independent mathematical comparison to the pinned original theorem excerpt in the Stage A record; source proofs/remarks not opened. Preliminary only.
statement:
For a ringed site (C,O), a complex E^bullet is **perfect** when after a covering of every site object it has a quasi-isomorphism from a **strictly perfect** complex (bounded, termwise direct summand of finite free O-modules); a derived object is perfect if represented by such a complex (source Definition perfect at 12734–12746). A perfect object is **not assumed globally bounded** unless the topos is quasi-compact. Its relation to pseudo-coherence and local finite Tor dimension is an equivalence only where stated, not an inherited hypothesis.

Let $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O})$ be a ringed site. Let $(K, L, M, f, g, h)$
be a distinguished triangle in $D(\mathcal{O})$. If two out of three of
$K, L, M$ are perfect then the third is also perfect.
hypotheses: (C,O) is a ringed site and K→L→M→K[1] is a distinguished triangle in D(O).
Any two among K,L,M are perfect.
conclusions: The remaining third object is perfect.
original_source_statement_tex:
\label{lemma-two-out-of-three-perfect}
Let $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O})$ be a ringed site. Let $(K, L, M, f, g, h)$
be a distinguished triangle in $D(\mathcal{O})$. If two out of three of
$K, L, M$ are perfect then the third is also perfect.
